comparator.name: Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology
comparator.sourceNotes: Current annual OER, articles1.1/8.2/9.4/9.5/9.6 controls. B1 and B2 each60EC compulsory; B3 free space30EC in semester1 and compulsory arts-based methods6EC, independent Research Project3(fieldwork)15EC, thesis9EC in semester2. Choose the genuine30EC course-choice space, not the optional18ECplacement+12ECcourses. B2 requires positive/deferred BSA; Statistics2 requires Statistics1 passed or assignments completed. ResearchProject2 requires Project1 passed and participatory methods passed or portfolio submitted. All120EC B1/B2 precede compulsoryB3semester2. Fieldwork requires approved project workplan and arts-based-methods attendance/portfolio; thesis assessed only after Project3 passed. OER3.11 also requires first-year RADAr-NL0EC, without exemption. Free choices cannot duplicate compulsory/exempted components; outside non-partner institutions require ExaminationBoard approval. Future prospective pages remain indicative; currentOER provides coherent current annual basis, not a guarantee of future offerings.

trace: introduces social organisation, inequality and sociological explanations of everyday life
traces modern historical changes in social institutions and global inequalities
teaches climate mechanisms underlying the programme’s human–nature and climate-justice questions

develops qualitative research design, data collection/interpretation, reflexivity and a group project; it supports inquiry into lived meanings without reproducing the full specialist ethnographic fieldwork sequence
examines how law shapes social justice and unequal treatment in institutions

develops social theory about modernity, inequality and colonial settings
examines imperial histories behind contemporary global power and development inequalities
analyses public narratives and political claims around climate justice

studies environmental-justice movements and their anti-colonial claims about unequal harm
examines international relations and global institutions implicated in development cooperation
studies West African material heritage, cultural meanings and appropriation through a specific regional case
examines moral claims about inequality and responsibilities in social and ecological change
examines civil society, solidarity and global social theory relevant to collective life

examines whose interests influence EU policy, a specific institutional case of unequal political power rather than a substitute for lived anthropology
examines violent conflict, its social consequences and approaches to peace in unequal societies
examines which actors influence the governance of sustainability and whose interests prevail

provides a specific complementary study of comparative property, contract and tort law and the social/economic pressures underlying legal principles; it is not an anthropology-of-kinship or debt course
studies documentary representation and research-based accounts of other people’s lives, without substituting for ethnographic fieldwork
introduces sustainability systems that underpin analysis of unequal environmental change
introduces biodiversity and ecological processes in human–nature relations
examines biodiversity conservation and choices affecting human relationships with nature
examines ecosystem functions affected by environmental change
analyses visual representations and public debate about environment and justice
examines natural hazards, risk and adaptation under uneven exposure
conducts collaborative research on a local sustainability problem with an external partner, while not reproducing ethnographic fieldwork

examines food production, global population needs, farming practices and environmental impacts, comparing sustainable alternatives; a specific food–environment contribution to human–nature inquiry

Actual memoir/autobiography/travel and migrant narratives examine memory, embodiment, agency, cultural identity and ethics of representation, using comparative close life-narrative analysis and writing; not ethnographic fieldwork.

alternatives.label: Social worlds, cultural meanings & inequality
alternatives.concept: A social and cultural inquiry programme combining sociological theory and empirical qualitative research with lived gender histories, Indigenous collaborative inquiry, life narratives, inequality, rights and global change. Interviews, participatory and visual methods and cultural interpretation sustain inquiry into lived meanings. It differs from Radboud’s full anthropological theory, kinship and independent ethnographic fieldwork and thesis formation.

progression: Actual current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites pass; first-year PPD,24unique180EC,fourperterm,advancedminimum. Foundationalrhetoric/data/empiricalmethods preferredbeforeadvancedapplications; no inventedformalprerequisites.

alternatives.label: Climate justice and human–nature relations
alternatives.concept: A programme examining human–nature relations through social theory, Indigenous history, environmental justice, rights and sustainability governance, supported by ecological science and sustainable food systems. Qualitative research and a local sustainability project provide empirical work; they do not reproduce Radboud’s independent ethnographic fieldwork.
alternatives.labelReason: A substantial environmental science sequence is linked to sociology, justice and governance rather than appearing as an incidental theme; the title names that actual combination.
alternatives.distinctness: Ninecourses67.5ECdifferent eachway. The broad option develops gender/modernhistory/lifenarratives/documentary and political/legal institutions; the environmental option adds physical/ecological foundations, biodiversity/conservation/ecosystems, hazards, sustainable farming and partner-based delta research. Both retain social theory, qualitative inquiry, Indigenous perspectives and justice, so the change concerns how unequal human–nature relations are investigated, not a new title alone.
progression: Actual current offerings and earlier formal prerequisites pass; first-year PPD,24unique180EC,fourperterm,advancedminimum. Foundationalrhetoric/data/empiricalmethods preferredbeforeadvancedapplications; no inventedformalprerequisites. Research in a Sustainable Delta is offered only2026Fall and is placed there with sociology and climate study. It has no formal prerequisite and its description supplies an advisor-supported research process; no prior ethnographic expertise is assumed. Sustainability Essentials and biodiversity precede later ecology/farming study. Early300level alone is not a failure gate.

candidates.label: Migration and multicultural belonging
candidates.reason: Actual migration/identity material in sociology, modern history, Indigenous family separation/resurgence, racial representation and the added migrant life-narrative course is recognized. These largely belong to the broad option already. Targeted travel-writing, comparative politics, constitutional law, negotiation and policy leads do not establish a separate sustained migration/mobility inquiry with enough qualitatively distinct curriculum; replacing lived study with generic law/politics would change the object. No absence-of-title or matching-course quota used.

selection.assessment: Two related programme-level responses retained after strengthening lived/cultural inquiry with actual migrant/life narratives, Indigenous co-created arts/PhotoVoice and participant observation. The broad option sustains sociological theory/qualitative empiricalwork and cultural meaning; the environmental option changes9courses67.5EC toward ecological mechanisms and unequal environment/justice/governance. Real ethnographic/participatory methods receive fullweight without equating them with required15EC independentfieldwork. Migrationleads assessed substantively but not manufactured as a third programme.

blocks: Both examine gender and power; UCR focuses on American cultural histories and lived experiences rather than a cross-cultural anthropology sequence.

Partial arts-based research correspondence: Indigenous storywork, relational inquiry, collaborative art and Photo/Voice with knowledge holders. UCR uses situated Indigenous historical inquiry rather than the complete anthropology fieldwork-preparation course.
Both use a specific region to study cultural meaning and colonial encounters; UCR focuses on West African heritage.
Both introduce social structures and inequality; Radboud integrates cultural and development perspectives.
Both examine societal change through sociological theory; Radboud combines this with more sustained anthropology.
Both engage with debates in social theory; Radboud has more dedicated anthropological scholarship.
Both consider international relationships and cooperation; UCR treats the field through political theory.

Partial power-and-participation correspondence in human–nature relations: stakeholder interests, justice and institutions shape sustainability decisions. UCR does not reproduce the full anthropology of materiality.
Both develop qualitative inquiry into social experience; UCR’s course is general sociological methodology.

Partial quantitative-method correspondence: inferential and multivariable models, experimental designs and R reporting. UCR does not reproduce the entire separately credited Radboud statistics sequence.
Both develop academic writing, research literacy and reflective formation. UCR also includes civic collaboration; the later Radboud research and professional components remain separately credited.
The selected UCR courses do not directly study kinship as a sustained anthropological subject.
A course in qualitative methods does not replace Radboud’s separately credited first-year research project.
The UCR statistics course is aligned to the subsequent statistics component; Radboud credits descriptive statistics separately.
UCR’s personal development course is shown elsewhere; this distinct socially engaged component has no direct credited match.

UCR qualitative research includes participatory video, visual approaches and team inquiry and is shown once with the first methods component. This separately credited participatory-methods course has no additional full course counterpart.
The selected UCR courses do not specifically study debt relations and financial behaviour.
Ethics is present in a UCR alternative, but it does not reproduce a philosophy-of-science course on knowledge and research.
The separate nine-credit participatory research project has no scheduled UCR fieldwork equivalent.

UCR sociology, migrant life narratives, Indigenous histories and racial representation examine belonging and exclusion in specific settings; no single selected course establishes the full comparative im/mobility component.
A stand-alone literature review is not present as an independent credited UCR component.
The second socially engaged learning component is separate from UCR’s first-year PPD.
Radboud’s nine-credit bachelor thesis is required; UCR optional research is a comparison-only option.
UCR includes team qualitative research, participant observation and situated collaborative inquiry. These do not establish Radboud’s compulsory15EC independent ethnographic fieldwork.
The thirty-credit Radboud free-choice space remains genuinely open and is not assigned invented courses.

notes.text: Radboud combines anthropology and development sociology with a specialist theory and methods sequence, independent fieldwork and a bachelor thesis. UCR can approach inequality, cultural meaning and human–nature relations through sociology, history, law, media and environmental study, but these courses do not constitute the full disciplinary fieldwork curriculum.

audience.programmeDescription: Radboud’s Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology studies cultural diversity, social inequality and how people understand and organise their lives. The degree combines social theory with qualitative, participatory and arts-based research, culminating in independent fieldwork and a bachelor thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR programmes offer related study of social worlds, cultural meanings, unequal power and human–nature relations. They combine sociology and empirical research with cultural history and other relevant fields. They do not reproduce Radboud’s specialist anthropology sequence, compulsory independent ethnographic fieldwork or bachelor thesis.

curriculum.limitation: Based on the current annual regulations. A required zero-credit Dutch academic-language test sits outside the 180 EC total. Future offerings and requirements may change.

componentNotes.y3-fieldwork: Compulsory 15 EC independent fieldwork. Requires all 120 EC from years 1–2, an approved workplan and completion of the arts-based-methods participation/portfolio requirements.
componentNotes.y3-thesis: Compulsory 9 EC thesis; assessed after Research Project3 is passed.
componentNotes.y3-free-choice: 30EC genuine elective-course space selected here. The optional18EC placement plus12EC courses is a separate permitted option. No duplicated compulsory/exempted credit. Study at another non-partner institution requires examination-board consent; an exchange requires all60first-yearEC.
componentNotes.y1-academic: First-year RADAr-NL academic language test carries0EC and is required without exemption. Normal first-year study-advice threshold42EC, subject to personal circumstances. Second-year study requires a positive or deferred advice decision.
componentNotes.y2-statistics-2: Requires Statistics1 passed or all its work assignments completed.
componentNotes.y2-project-2: Requires ResearchProject1 passed and ParticipatoryMethods passed or its portfolio submitted.
componentNotes.y3-creative-methods: All120EC from years1–2 are required before compulsory second-semester year3 courses. Fieldwork starts after an approved workplan and the arts-based-methods attendance/portfolio conditions.
